top_picks.name: Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and today is a quiet, useful demonstration of why. VOO holds the 500 largest US companies for a rock-bottom 0.03% fee. It closed at 707.60, down 0.19%, on a day when the index it tracks barely moved but the tape underneath it was violent in both directions: Astera Labs fell 11.96%, AMD fell 7.04% despite a record quarter, Credo fell 5.59%, SanDisk fell 5.40% and Western Digital 5.36%, while Eli Lilly rose 4.86%, Arista rose 3.57% and Nvidia rose 3.43%. Owning all 500 meant that entire spread netted out to a rounding error for you. VOO sits at 96% of its 30-day range and about 3.1% above its 50-day average, and it has logged just one distribution day in the trailing window against three for SPY and six for the Nasdaq proxy, which says the broad index is not the part of this market institutions are selling.
top_picks.why_now: Because the market is narrowing, and narrowing markets are exactly what a broad index is for. The Dow made a record while the Nasdaq fell 0.8%, semiconductors are 4.4% below their 50-day, and leadership has rotated into healthcare, electrical equipment and steel. You do not have to identify that rotation in advance if you own all of it. The macro setup also improved at the margin today: oil fell, the 10-year eased toward 4.6%, and September hike odds came down to roughly 57% from 67%.
top_picks.risk: A near-record high with a live September rate hike is the risk, and the concentration underneath it is the other. VOO is about a third mega-cap technology, so the AI complex is a much larger share of your outcome than 'the whole market' suggests. If the Aug 12 CPI print runs hot, or the Hormuz deal that has driven two sessions of oil relief falls apart, the index gives back quickly. Today it was insulated because losses in chips were offset by gains in healthcare and industrials; that offset is not guaranteed to hold.

grade.note: Unchanged at the top. The case for the core got quietly stronger today rather than weaker: the index absorbed an 11.96% collapse in one holding and a 7.04% drop in another and still finished essentially flat, which is diversification doing precisely the job you bought it for. One distribution day in the trailing window is the cleanest reading on the board. Best Sharpe of the three at plain market risk, the lowest historical drawdown, a 13.4% ten-year CAGR, and roughly 23% odds of a down year. The standing caveat: 96% of its 30-day range is a worse entry than a flush, so this stays a keep-buying-on-schedule holding rather than an all-at-once one.

top_picks.bear_case: The whole index falls 20% to 35% in a genuine bear market (it did about -32% across 2020 and 2022). The specific live risk: because roughly a third of the S&P is mega-cap tech, and that buildout is increasingly financed with debt, a September Fed hike plus a capex disappointment is a double hit the index cannot diversify away. Today's offsetting rotation into healthcare and industrials only works while those groups have room to run, and several of them (Eaton, Atkore, Hubbell, Nucor, WESCO) already closed at the very top of their 30-day ranges. The Monte Carlo 5th-percentile one-year outcome is about -15%, and a 2022-style year is closer to -25% to -32%. The saving grace: it has always recovered given time, which is exactly why you dollar-cost-average rather than lump in.

top_picks.name: Eli Lilly
top_picks.thesis: You asked me to flag a good pharma buy when one shows up, and today the thesis was tested by an actual earnings report and passed. Lilly reported second-quarter revenue up about 48% to nearly $23 billion, adjusted earnings above $8 a share, and raised full-year sales guidance to $85 billion to $87 billion. Mounjaro revenue rose 91% to $9.94 billion and Zepbound rose 123% to $4.26 billion. Lilly closed up 4.86% at 1,169.86 on 2.66 times its average volume, the heaviest genuine accumulation on the entire board, and healthcare was the best-performing group on either sheet at +1.50% while the XLV basket rose 1.27% on 1.59 times volume. The competitive picture improved at the same time: Novo Nordisk's CagriSema failed to control blood sugar as well as Lilly's tirzepatide in a head-to-head trial and its Wegovy pill came in short, leaving Lilly with 60.9% of the US obesity and diabetes market against Novo's 38.8%.
top_picks.why_now: Because this is the rare case where the business got better and the stock is still not extended. Even after a 4.86% jump, Lilly sits at only 52% of its 30-day range and 1.47% above its 50-day average, so you are not buying a vertical chart. Healthcare is also becoming genuine leadership rather than a hiding place: it was the only group with both a strong average gain and heavy confirming volume today, while the AI complex sold off on light volume. The policy calendar is known rather than a surprise: comments on the third Medicare negotiation cycle close Aug 17 and any negotiated prices take effect January 2028.
top_picks.risk: Valuation is still the main one: a rich multiple leaves little room for a trial disappointment or a competitor surprise. Policy is the second: the third Medicare negotiation cycle is live through 2026 and reaches Part B drugs for the first time, and Lilly's Trulicity is on the selected list. Third, buying immediately after a 4.86% earnings pop means you are paying up relative to anyone who bought last week, and single-quarter strength does not repeat on demand. Note also that Novo, the direct competitor, still carries two heavy liquidation events and sits at 3% of its 30-day range, a reminder of how fast sentiment turns on a single trial readout in this category.
sources: Lilly climbs, Novo falls as obesity drug battle intensifies
Eli Lilly stock surges after Q2 earnings beat driven by Mounjaro, Zepbound

grade.note: Upgraded from A-. The A- was held back by two specific doubts, and this quarter addressed both. The growth was in question: revenue rose 48%, the full-year guide went up to $85 billion to $87 billion, and the two GLP-1 franchises grew 91% and 123%. The competitive threat was the other: Novo's CagriSema lost a head-to-head trial on blood-sugar control and its oral Wegovy missed, and Lilly's US share widened to 60.9% against 38.8%. The stock backed it with the best volume confirmation on the board at 2.66 times average. What still keeps this from being the top pick is price: a premium multiple, a 30.9% ten-year CAGR that is already well understood by the market, and the Medicare negotiation cycle running through 2026 with Trulicity selected.

top_picks.bear_case: Two real threats. Policy: Medicare negotiation now reaches Part B drugs for the first time, Trulicity is on the third-cycle list, and the first round produced negotiated prices 38% to 79% below prior prices, so the eventual margin effect is not trivial even though it lands in 2028. Competition and valuation: you are paying a premium multiple for continued dominance, so any share loss to a Novo comeback, a safety signal, or a manufacturing stumble in the GLP-1 ramp hits hard. The simulation's 5th-percentile one-year outcome is about -21%, worse than VOO's, because a single stock carries single-name risk the ETF diversifies away. The cushions: 60.9% US share, a raised full-year guide, a very high return on equity, and a low beta that softens broad selloffs.

top_picks.factors: Political: drug-pricing policy is the standing risk, with the third Medicare negotiation cycle live and Trulicity selected, though negotiated prices do not bite until 2028. Environmental and structural: an aging, higher-weight population is a decade-long demand tailwind for obesity and diabetes drugs that runs independent of the economic cycle, the AI-capex cycle and the oil price. That independence is the entire reason healthcare is on this board, and today it paid: healthcare rose while chips, memory, photonics and the neoclouds all fell.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: Entry at the 1,169.86 close sits just 1.47% above the 50-day and at the middle of the 30-day range, which is a reasonable place to add even straight after an earnings pop. The stop near 988 and the take-profit near 1,876 produce the best risk-reward on the board at about 3.9 to 1. The Monte Carlo puts roughly 19% odds of a loss over one year and a median gain near 31%, with a worst modelled case near a 21% drawdown at the 5th percentile, so size it expecting a bad year to look like that, not like a wipeout.

top_picks.name: VanEck Semiconductor ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and semiconductors are the beating heart of your AI-infrastructure thesis. SMH holds the 25 biggest chip names (Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom, AMD, ASML, Micron and the rest) in one 0.35% fund, so you own the layer without guessing which chip wins the next socket. Today showed exactly why the basket beats the single name: AMD fell 7.04% on a record quarter, Astera Labs fell 11.96%, Credo fell 5.59% and SanDisk fell 5.40%, yet Nvidia rose 3.43% and Broadcom held flat, so the fund lost only 1.04%. It closed at 569.70, at 61% of its 30-day range and about 4.4% below its 50-day average. The demand side of the thesis is unchanged: the four largest hyperscalers have guided 2026 capital spending to roughly $725 billion between them, up about 77% from last year, with roughly three-quarters of that aimed at AI infrastructure.
top_picks.why_now: Because the price is still below trend while the order book keeps growing, and because today's selling was notably unenthusiastic: SMH fell on just 0.47 times its average volume, less than half a normal day's participation. Light-volume declines are a shortage of buyers rather than institutions dumping. The honest caveat is that this remains the most damaged corner of the board on a distribution-day basis, with nine on the fund and eleven on SanDisk, so 'below trend' here reflects real institutional selling earlier in the cycle, not just a quiet drift.
top_picks.risk: The expectations bar is the immediate risk, and AMD proved it today: a record $11.54 billion quarter, revenue up 50%, data-center revenue up 107%, third-quarter guidance near $13 billion, and the stock fell 7.04% anyway because it had already risen about 140% this year. When good news is not good enough, the problem is price rather than business. Underneath that, memory is the soft spot: SanDisk sits 20.66% below its 50-day with eleven distribution days and reported after today's close, Micron is 8.13% below its 50-day with seven, and any efficiency breakthrough that lets AI models do more with less memory attacks the strongest part of the current chip thesis.

grade.note: Held at B-. Nothing about the demand case broke today, and the fund's own behaviour was reassuring: it absorbed a 7% drop in AMD and a 12% drop in Astera Labs and lost only 1.04%, on less than half its average volume. But three things keep the grade where it is. Distribution days are still nine, the highest cluster on the board alongside SOXX at eight. It is 4.4% below its 50-day, so the trend is not repaired. And AMD's reaction is a warning that the whole group is now priced for very good news, which raises the cost of any disappointment. The best prices remain behind us. Keep scaling in on weakness rather than chasing.

top_picks.bear_case: The AI-capex cycle could be over-building just as efficiency gains reduce how much hardware each workload needs. That second thread is the underrated one: compression and quantization research aimed at cutting the memory footprint of large models has been circulating since the spring, and analysts have repeatedly revisited DRAM demand forecasts because of it. If models get cheaper to run faster than demand grows, the memory squeeze that is currently powering this thesis unwinds. Add custom silicon challenging Nvidia's position, China building its own supply chain, hyperscaler free cash flow compressing, and a buildout increasingly funded with debt just as the Fed flirts with a hike. It is concentrated and high-beta, so a market-wide risk-off takes it down harder than the index, and past cycles saw about -45% peak-to-trough. The simulation's 5th-percentile one-year outcome is about -18% and the worst path is far uglier. The offset: committed capex is still rising toward $725 billion, and nobody has cut.

Environmental and structural: semiconductors sit at the top of the AI buildout and customer capex guides are still rising, which is why the demand case survives a soft tape. The near-term swing factor is the rate path, because this is the longest-duration equity exposure on the board, which is why September hike odds falling to roughly 57% today was quietly helpful.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: Entry at the 569.70 close is 4.4% below the 50-day, so you are still buying below trend. The Monte Carlo still shows the lowest one-year loss odds of the three at about 17% with a median gain near 33%, which is the statistical case for owning the volatility rather than avoiding it.

top_picks_note: Not a buy list, a research shortlist. The three names are unchanged, because a mid-week session is not a reason to churn a long-term shortlist: one diversified core (VOO), one quality healthcare compounder outside the AI theme (LLY), and one diversified way to own the AI hardware layer (SMH). The one grade change is Lilly, from A- to A, and it was earned by results rather than by price action: revenue up 48%, full-year guidance raised to $85 billion to $87 billion, US obesity and diabetes share widening to 60.9% while Novo's CagriSema lost a head-to-head trial, and the heaviest confirming volume on the board at 2.66 times average. Established nuclear infrastructure remains the strongest candidate for a future slot and got more interesting again today: Vistra, Dominion, PSEG and Entergy all closed at the very bottom of their 30-day ranges while the contracts underneath them keep getting longer. It is not being added yet because the group has been falling for weeks and there is no sign the selling is finished, and buying into an active downtrend is different from buying a dip. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy today.

insights.title: A down day almost nobody participated in, and the heavy volume that did show up was two-sided
insights.body: Forty-five of 70 names closed lower, yet this was one of the least committed selloffs the board has recorded. The volume tells the story: SPY fell 0.20% on 0.90 times its average volume, the Nasdaq proxy QQQ fell 0.90% on 0.77x, and the semiconductor fund SMH fell 1.04% on just 0.47x, less than half a normal session. Across all 21 ETFs on the shelf there were zero heavy liquidation events in the trailing five sessions, down from several yesterday, and only seven of the 70 individual names carry one at all (AMD, Astera Labs, Vistra, Southern, Apple, Meta and Novo Nordisk, the last with two). That is a dramatic improvement from the 24 names carrying heavy events a session ago. Where real money did move, it moved in both directions and for specific reasons. The buying: Eli Lilly rose 4.86% on 2.66 times average volume after raising guidance, Arista rose 3.57% on 2.66x, Atkore traded 3.44x average, Nucor 1.71x, and the healthcare basket XLV rose 1.27% on 1.59x. The selling: Astera Labs fell 11.96% on 2.05x, AMD fell 7.04% on 1.75x after a record quarter, Alphabet fell 4.03% on 1.49x, and Palantir fell 2.60% on 1.45x. What has not improved is the distribution-day count, which measures accumulated institutional selling rather than one session: SanDisk 11, TSMC 9, Cameco 9, Vistra 8, Oracle 8, Intel 8, and at the fund level SMH 9, SOXX 8 and VGT 8 against just one for VOO.
insights.matters: For a long-term investor the useful distinction is between a market being sold and a market simply not being bought, and today was firmly the second. Light-volume declines retrace far more easily than heavy-volume ones, and the near-total disappearance of heavy liquidation events is the single most constructive datapoint on the page. But do not read it as an all-clear: the distribution-day counts say institutions did real selling in semis, memory and the utilities over recent weeks, and that damage is still on the charts. The practical takeaway is that this is a fine day to make a scheduled purchase and a poor day to make a large opportunistic one, because nothing was on sale, it was just quiet.

insights.title: AMD delivered a record quarter and fell 7%, which tells you the bar, not the business, is the problem
insights.body: AMD reported record revenue of $11.54 billion, up 50% year over year and ahead of the $11.31 billion consensus, with adjusted earnings of $1.66 a share against $1.62 expected. Data-center revenue was $6.7 billion, up 107% year over year, and now supplies 58% of company sales on the back of EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators. Third-quarter guidance came in near $13 billion. The stock fell 7.04% on 1.75 times average volume and now sits 6.33% below its 50-day average with a heavy liquidation event in its trailing window. The reason is arithmetic rather than analysis: AMD had already risen roughly 140% this year going into the print, so a beat of that size was the minimum required rather than a surprise. The same pattern repeated across the AI hardware complex. Astera Labs fell 11.96% on 2.05 times volume, Credo fell 5.59%, Super Micro fell 4.32% and the neoclouds fell (Nebius 2.99%, CoreWeave 2.19%). Nvidia was the exception, rising 3.43% to close at the very top of its 30-day range and 6.54% above its 50-day. Chip equipment fell 2.21% as a group, with KLA now 12.97% below its 50-day and Lam Research 9.13% below.
insights.matters: This is the single most important lesson on the page for a long-term investor, and it costs people money every quarter: a great business and a great stock outcome are different things when expectations have already run. Nothing in AMD's quarter weakened the AI-infrastructure thesis, and data-center revenue more than doubling is direct confirmation of it. What the reaction tells you is that the chip layer is now priced for excellence, so the margin of safety has thinned even though the fundamentals improved. That argues for the basket over the single name (SMH lost only 1.04% while AMD lost 7.04%), and for adding on the quiet, disappointing days rather than into earnings.

insights.title: Healthcare was the best group on the board, and for once it was leadership rather than shelter
insights.body: Healthcare and pharma rose 1.50% on average, the strongest of the fifteen groups on either sheet, and the XLV basket rose 1.27% on 1.59 times average volume. That volume detail matters: it was the only sector-level advance today backed by above-average participation, while the AI complex fell on unusually thin trade. Eli Lilly drove it, rising 4.86% on 2.66 times volume after reporting revenue up about 48% to nearly $23 billion, adjusted earnings above $8 a share, and a full-year sales guide raised to $85 billion to $87 billion. Mounjaro rose 91% to $9.94 billion and Zepbound rose 123% to $4.26 billion. The competitive gap widened at the same time: Novo Nordisk's CagriSema failed to match Lilly's tirzepatide on blood-sugar control in a head-to-head trial and its oral Wegovy came in short of estimates, leaving Lilly with 60.9% of the US obesity and diabetes market against Novo's 38.8%. The rest of the group joined in: UnitedHealth rose 1.28%, Johnson & Johnson 1.04%, AbbVie 0.98% and Merck 0.26%. The catch is that most of them are rising from depressed levels rather than strength, with AbbVie at 12% of its 30-day range, UnitedHealth at 18% and Novo at 3%.
insights.matters: Healthcare is on this board specifically as the reminder that good businesses exist outside the AI trade, and today it did the harder version of that job: not merely holding up while chips fell, but attracting real money. For a long-term investor the interesting structural point is that Lilly's growth is driven by demographics and drug efficacy, which have nothing to do with hyperscaler capital spending, the oil price or the September rate decision. That genuine independence is worth more in a portfolio than a slightly higher expected return that happens to be correlated with everything else you own. For a diversified holding XLV covers pharma, insurers and devices in one line; for a single name Lilly is the growth-plus-defence pick, with the understanding that you are now paying up for a business that just proved it deserves to be paid up for.

insights.title: Memory was the worst group on the board again, and the efficiency question is the thread to watch
insights.body: Memory and storage fell 3.57%, the weakest group on either sheet, with SanDisk down 5.40% and Western Digital down 5.36% while Micron finished essentially flat at +0.06%. SanDisk remains the most technically damaged name on the board by a wide margin: eleven distribution days, 20.66% below its 50-day average, and at just 37% of its 30-day range. It reported fourth-quarter results after today's close, so that reaction is not yet in these prices. The fundamental case has not changed and remains genuinely strong: DRAM contract prices are set to rise 50% to 55% this quarter against the fourth quarter of 2025, HBM is effectively sold out for 2026 with Micron's capacity committed through 2027, and Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron control over 95% of global DRAM while having reallocated capacity toward high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. The counter-argument that deserves attention is efficiency. Compression research aimed at shrinking the memory footprint of large AI models, most prominently Google's TurboQuant work published in the spring, has already prompted analysts to revisit DRAM demand forecasts more than once. The considered view from the industry press is that it is a meaningful optimisation rather than a solution, since it does not reduce model size, training cost, networking or storage, and one analysis argued it could raise memory demand overall by making AI inference cheaper to deploy widely.
insights.matters: This is the most uncomfortable and most common situation a long-term investor faces: the fundamentals say earnings are coming, the chart says institutions have been selling for weeks, and both are true at once. The reconciliation is usually time rather than a clean bottom. What is worth genuinely watching, as opposed to worrying about, is the efficiency thread, because it is the one development that could break the memory thesis rather than merely delay it. If models get cheaper to run faster than AI demand grows, the shortage ends early. That is an argument for owning memory inside a broad chip basket such as SOXX or SMH, which hold Micron, SanDisk and Western Digital alongside Nvidia and Broadcom, rather than concentrating in the memory makers themselves. SK Hynix, the HBM leader, trades only in Seoul, so a basket is the only route most US investors have to it anyway.

insights.title: Oil kept falling, the 10-year eased, and the odds of a September hike came down with them
insights.body: The energy story that has driven this market for two weeks moved further in the helpful direction. President Trump said an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, closed since April, could be reached imminently, saying it 'could happen. Tomorrow or the next day.' Brent held above $79 and WTI settled near $75, well below the roughly $84 WTI peak on Jul 29. The rates market responded: the 10-year Treasury yield eased toward 4.6%, down from the 4.70% that the macro chip still shows for Aug 3, and markets trimmed the probability of a September rate hike to roughly 57% from about 67% a day earlier. The Fed itself has not moved. It held at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 in a 9-to-3 vote, its most divided decision since 2016, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan all dissenting in favour of a hike. The 2-year sits at 4.25%, leaving the 10Y-2Y curve positively sloped by about 0.45, and the VIX closed near 16.5, a calm reading. Underneath the noise, inflation continues to improve: June CPI was 3.5% year over year (down from 4.2%), core 2.6% (down from 2.8%), and unemployment 4.2%. Note that the oil chip on the macro strip still reads $84.25 from Jul 27 because FRED publishes with a lag and has not caught the last two sessions.
insights.matters: Rates are the single biggest input to what your holdings are worth, because the 10-year is the yardstick every other asset is priced against. The setup into the Aug 12 CPI print keeps improving: cheaper crude feeds directly into a softer headline number, and a soft print takes the September hike off the table entirely. Two cautions keep this from being a reason to press. First, the Hormuz deal is a statement of intent, not a signature, and if it collapses both oil and hike odds go straight back up. Second, a September meeting that publishes the dot plot carries more information than a normal one, so the market reaction can be larger than the decision itself warrants. The practical response is unchanged: add on a schedule rather than making one large bet before Aug 12, and take some comfort that a 10-year near 4.6% still pays you to be patient.
sources: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500 climb as Trump says Hormuz deal is close

insights.title: The regulated utilities are pinned at their lows while uranium is being bought, and that split is the tell
insights.body: Nuclear infrastructure and power majors fell 1.11%, and the weakness is concentrated in one specific place. Four of the ten names closed at the very bottom of their 30-day range (Vistra at 0%, Dominion at 0%, PSEG at 0% and Entergy at 0%), with Southern at 4%, meaning five of the six names sitting at 30-day lows anywhere on the entire board are power companies. Vistra is 9.86% below its 50-day with eight distribution days, Talen 12.01% below, BWX Technologies 9.69% below with seven. This is a weeks-long trend rather than a single bad session. Uranium went the other way: Cameco rose 1.27%, the URA basket rose 0.94% on 2.01 times average volume, the heaviest volume of any ETF on the shelf, and Centrus sits at 96% of its 30-day range and 9.74% above its 50-day. The contracted demand underneath the equities has not weakened. Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta have signed nuclear power agreements totalling close to 10 gigawatts during 2026, Constellation's 20-year Meta deal supplies 1.1 gigawatts from Clinton starting 2027, and Talen expanded its Amazon agreement to as much as 1.9 gigawatts through at least 2042.
insights.matters: The divergence is the useful signal: money is buying the fuel and selling the power producers. The most likely explanation is rate sensitivity rather than a nuclear problem, because regulated utilities are bond proxies and the 10-year has climbed from about 4.49% a month ago to the mid-4s, which mechanically pressures anything owned for its dividend. That distinction matters for a long-term investor, because a business whose stock falls due to the discount rate is very different from one whose customers are leaving. These companies have twenty-year contracts with the best-capitalised buyers on earth. If the September hike comes off the table, this is the group with the most room to recover, and it is currently the cheapest part of the board on a distance-from-trend basis. The internal split is worth knowing: merchant operators (Constellation, Vistra, Talen) carry the upside and the power-price risk, while the regulated names (Dominion, Southern, PSEG, Entergy) pay dividends and earn a regulated return. NLR is the utility-heavy nuclear basket, URA the purer uranium-miner version.
sources: AI companies have signed enough nuclear deals to power 7 million homes and uranium stocks are surging
Constellation, Vistra and PSEG could be next to ink nuclear-data center supply deals
AI Data Center Power Deals and Nuclear Expansion Could Be A Game Changer For Constellation Energy

insights.title: Quantum and space led the decline, and a share unlock is why the space names have been falling
insights.body: Sheet 2 was the weak half of the board. Quantum pure-plays fell 3.48%, the second-worst group anywhere, with IonQ down 4.29% and now 19.45% below its 50-day, Rigetti down 3.84% and Quantum Computing Inc down 3.79%. The space names held up better on the day (Rocket Lab +0.46%, Intuitive Machines +0.21%, AST SpaceMobile -2.74%) but the damage is in the trend rather than the session: the UFO space basket is 7.2% below its 50-day, Intuitive Machines is 35.72% below its own and Rocket Lab 19.76% below. There is a specific, identifiable mechanical cause. SpaceX shares fell about 13% today after results in which an earnings beat was overshadowed by elevated AI capital spending, and its post-IPO lockup expires Aug 6, increasing the tradable share count by more than 140%, with further releases scheduled for December 2026 and June 2027. A supply increase of that size in the sector's anchor stock drags the smaller names with it regardless of their own progress. The AI neoclouds also fell, with Nebius down 2.99% carrying seven distribution days and CoreWeave down 2.19%.
insights.matters: This is a reminder of what Sheet 2 is for and how to size it. These are venture-style positions where a single scheduled event, in this case a lockup expiry that has been on the calendar for months, can move the entire group more than any operational result. That is the opposite of the durable, contract-backed cash flows on Sheet 1. None of it argues that quantum computing or commercial space are bad long-term themes, and Rocket Lab's Neutron debut is still targeted for the fourth quarter. It argues that the position size should be one where a 35% drawdown, which Intuitive Machines is currently delivering, does not change how you feel about the rest of your portfolio. If you want the theme without the single-name risk, QTUM and UFO are the baskets, and both are also below their 50-day averages.
sources: SpaceX Craters on Soaring AI Costs; Space-Sector Peers Decline
Space Stocks Got Crushed on SpaceX's Big Day. Is the Sell-Off a Warning or a Buying Opportunity?

smart_money.intro: Where the large, well-informed pools of money are actually positioned, read from the three sources a private investor can legitimately see: weekly CFTC futures positioning, published reports of Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage flow (the desk data itself is proprietary, so this is press reporting rather than a primary feed), and disclosed policy and corporate spending. It is a timing signal, not a guarantee, and institutions are wrong regularly. Treat it as context for when to add to a position you already believe in, never as the reason to own it.

items.title: Leverage is back near records, and the cushion that made the last bounce easy has largely been spent
items.body: Reported Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage data describes a full round trip completed over about eight weeks. Through mid-July, hedge funds sold US technology at a record pace, acting as net sellers in six of eight weeks, with mega-cap tech exposure falling to its lowest point of the year and semiconductors leading the outflows. Since then the money has come back: net long exposure to global information technology posted its biggest increase in more than five years, and positioning is back near the highest levels since the bank began tracking these trades in 2016. The leverage picture is the part worth dwelling on. Gross leverage across the full prime book rose for a third consecutive year to a record by the end of 2025, and net leverage now sits near three-year highs, with US long-short net leverage reported at 55.3%, in the top 11% of readings over the past year. Magnificent 7 names account for roughly 19% of total US net exposure, up from about 11% in early April though still below the 21% peak of mid-2024. Alongside the re-leveraging, higher inflation readings and climbing bond yields have pushed managers to add downside protection, so hedging activity has risen even as the long positions were rebuilt.
items.matters: Positioning explains a great deal of what this board has done and what it is likely to do next. An emptied book is why a chip rally could run on half the usual volume a week ago; a rebuilt book is why today's decline needed so little selling pressure to happen. When leverage is near records and the crowd is concentrated in the same mega-cap names, the market becomes more sensitive to any shock, because leveraged holders are forced to sell rather than choosing to. That is not a forecast of a decline, and crowded positioning can stay crowded for a long time. It is an argument for two specific habits: keep buying in tranches rather than lumps so a fast drawdown is an opportunity rather than a problem, and resist adding to whatever the crowd is most concentrated in, which right now is the mega-cap AI complex.
sources: 2026 Hedge Fund Industry Outlook: Generation Alpha
Goldman says hedge funds sell US tech stocks at record pace
Hedge Funds Pile Back Into AI and Tech Stocks

items.title: Positioning data is unchanged this session: still the Jul 28 report, with the next update due Aug 7
items.body: The CFTC publishes Traders in Financial Futures weekly on a Friday, so today's figures are identical to yesterday's and still describe the week ended Jul 28. Nothing below has moved; the next refresh lands Aug 7 and will be the first read that includes this week's rally and pullback. As of Jul 28: in S&P 500 e-mini futures, asset managers were heavily net long at 944,770 contracts (47.6% of open interest), adding 15,611 on the week, while leveraged funds stayed net short 297,476 but bought back 25,389 contracts of that short. In the Nasdaq-100, leveraged funds cut their net short by 16,392 contracts to 58,298 while asset managers added 4,134. The 10-year Treasury note remains the most polarised contract on the list: asset managers net long 2,611,964 contracts and leveraged funds net short 2,155,739, with the leveraged side adding a further 90,934 contracts to that short during the week, a direct bet that yields go higher. In VIX futures, leveraged funds increased their net short by 15,387 contracts, a bet that volatility stays low.
items.matters: Two things follow from this. The first is a caution about staleness: this data was collected nine days ago, before the Hormuz headlines, before the Aug 4 rally and before today's rotation, so treat it as where the fast money was rather than where it is. The second is the standing read, which has not changed: cover the equity shorts, stay short bonds, sell volatility. That combination has been profitable so far, with the VIX near 16.5 and yields elevated. It is also crowded and fragile, because all three legs lose money at once if the Aug 12 CPI print moves rates sharply in either direction. Watch the Aug 7 release specifically for whether the leveraged 10-year short got any smaller as yields eased this week, because a cover there would be the clearest sign the hike trade is being unwound.
sources: CFTC Commitments of Traders, Traders in Financial Futures

items.title: The optical-module ban is now in drafting, and the supply-chain risk runs in both directions
items.body: The proposed US restriction on Chinese-made optical transceiver modules moved from headline to drafting this week, with the FCC leading preparation of rules that would bar new Chinese optical modules from US data centers on national-security grounds, citing risks of data theft, malware and service disruption, and officials aiming to finalise and enforce within the year. Reporting today emphasised the mutual nature of the exposure: the US depends on Chinese optical manufacturing capacity that cannot be replaced quickly, and industry analysis notes that contract manufacturers such as Fabrinet, Sanmina and Jabil would need massive capacity investment plus confidence the rules will not reverse in six months, with the sector already supply-constrained. Today the optics names gave back part of yesterday's surge, with photonics down 2.18% as a group (Lumentum -2.73%, Credo -5.59%, Applied Optoelectronics -2.33%) while Coherent rose 1.39% and held the top of its 30-day range. Separately, comments on the third Medicare drug price negotiation cycle close Aug 17, the first cycle to reach Part B drugs. The standing government positions are unchanged: Washington holds equity in Intel, MP Materials and Lithium Americas and is the anchor customer for Centrus, BWX Technologies, Rocket Lab and Palantir.
items.matters: Yesterday the optics chain rose as much as 21% on this proposal; today it fell back. That round trip inside 48 hours, with no change in the underlying rule, is the clearest possible demonstration that policy-driven moves are repricings of probability rather than of business value. Nothing has been enacted, and trade rules of this kind are frequently softened. The discipline is to let policy adjust your sizing but never form your thesis: prefer businesses that would work without the rule and get helped by it (Coherent, Fabrinet, Corning) over ones whose case depends on it, and treat a policy jump as a prompt to review a position rather than to buy one at a 20% premium.
sources: US Drafts Ban on Chinese Optical Modules, Exposing Mutual Supply Chain Risks
FCC Ban on New Chinese Optical Modules
CMS Announces Manufacturer Participation in Third Cycle of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

items.title: About $725 billion of committed spending is the floor under every supplier on Sheet 1, and Meta raised again
items.body: The four largest buyers of AI infrastructure have guided 2026 capital spending to roughly $725 billion between them, up about 77% from last year's record $410 billion, with roughly three-quarters of the total, near $450 billion, aimed specifically at AI infrastructure. On the same tally, Amazon is near $200 billion, Alphabet $175 billion to $185 billion, Meta $125 billion to $145 billion and Microsoft $110 billion to $120 billion. Per-company figures vary between sources because of differing fiscal-year conventions, so the aggregate is the more reliable number. The newest change is Meta, which raised its full-year range to $125 billion to $145 billion from a prior $115 billion to $135 billion, and the stated reason is worth reading closely: higher component pricing and additional data-center costs, not additional capacity. That is the memory shortage appearing in a customer's cost line. Hyperscale operators continue to say they cannot keep pace with demand for AI capacity. Investor patience is visibly thinner than the spending, though: Alphabet fell 4.03% today on 1.49 times average volume, with reporting pointing to antitrust remedy risk and margin pressure from exactly this capital spending.
items.matters: For a long-term holder this remains the most concrete number on the page, because it is committed spending rather than a forecast, and it converts directly into revenue for the chip, memory, server, optics, electrical and power names on Sheet 1. It is also the number to watch for the first genuine crack. The theme does not break when a supplier misses a quarter, and it did not break today when AMD fell 7% on a record quarter. It breaks when a hyperscaler cuts this figure. Nobody has cut, and Meta just raised. Until that changes, weakness in the suppliers is more likely to be positioning and valuation than a change in demand, which is precisely the situation in which scheduled buying beats waiting for clarity.
sources: Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon capex spending to hit $725 billion in 2026, up 77%
Hyperscalers Hit $700 Billion in 2026 AI Spending Plans
Amazon, Meta and Microsoft face skeptical investors after Google report sparked sell-off

primer.intro: A large AI data center is a machine built in physical layers, and money flows into it from the top (the customers who order it) down through every supplier who makes a piece. Here is where the dollars land, and why the least glamorous layers can be the safest way to invest.

sections.h: Start at the top: the customers
sections.p: The hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle) announce the giant spending budgets, now roughly $725B in 2026, that everyone else competes to capture. Owning them is the most diversified way to own the theme, because their core businesses (ads, cloud, software) fund the AI bet and keep earning even if AI spending pauses. Two cautions: the market now scrutinizes the return on that capex, and the group is increasingly tapping external financing, which makes the whole chain more rate-sensitive. Meta's latest raise was attributed to higher component prices rather than more capacity, which is a cost increase dressed as an investment increase.

Nvidia (NVDA) designs the GPUs that do the AI math; AMD (AMD) is the challenger; Broadcom (AVGO) builds the custom chips hyperscalers increasingly design in-house, a trend now challenging Nvidia's near-monopoly. None own factories: TSMC (TSM) prints the chips using machines only ASML (ASML) makes, and every GPU needs memory from Micron (MU). Highest growth, highest risk, and the layer that falls first on any overcapacity or competition scare. It is also now the layer priced for perfection: AMD grew data-center revenue 107% and the stock still fell 7%.

Memory deserves its own line. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron control over 95% of global DRAM and have shifted a large majority of combined output to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. That has sent AI memory pricing sharply higher and left consumer-grade memory scarce, which is a margin tailwind for MU, SNDK and WDC and a cost shock for every device maker. It makes this the most cyclical layer of the buildout. The live question is efficiency: compression techniques that shrink the memory footprint of AI models could either soften the shortage or, by making inference cheaper, spread AI workloads widely enough to increase memory demand overall. SK Hynix is Seoul-listed, so US investors reach it mainly through the baskets.

sections.h: Layer 2: The box and the room
sections.p: The chips get assembled into servers by Super Micro (SMCI) and Dell (DELL). A rack of AI chips runs blazing hot, so it needs advanced cooling and power distribution from Vertiv (VRT), and fast switches from Arista (ANET) to connect racks together. This is the guts of the room, and these are project businesses whose revenue lands unevenly quarter to quarter, which is why single-day moves of 10% or more are routine here in both directions.

AI splits one job across thousands of chips, so they must talk at the speed of light over fiber. Transceivers and lasers come from Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE), long-haul interconnect from Ciena (CIEN), and the actual glass fiber from Corning (GLW). Optics content rises with every hardware generation as 800G gives way to 1.6T. This layer is now also a policy battleground, with a draft US rule targeting Chinese-made optical modules, which cuts both ways: it hands domestic suppliers pricing power while exposing how much capacity sits offshore.

The least glamorous and often most attractive layer: switchgear from Eaton (ETN) and Hubbell (HUBB), the steel and PVC conduit that carries every wire from Atkore (ATKR), jobsite supply from WESCO (WCC), transmission and substation build from Quanta (PWR), and the raw steel from Nucor (NUE). Physical, hard-to-substitute, multi-year backlogs. This was the only Sheet 1 group to finish higher today, and five of its six names closed at or near the top of their 30-day ranges.

A data center is useless without electricity, and AI has made power the true bottleneck. Existing-reactor operators signing long deals are Constellation (CEG), Vistra (VST) and Talen (TLN); the regulated fleet owners are Dominion (D), Southern (SO), PSEG (PEG) and Entergy (ETR); fuel comes from Cameco (CCJ) and Centrus (LEU); reactor and SMR technology from BWX (BWXT), Oklo (OKLO) and NuScale (SMR); and near-term gas-turbine and grid power from GE Vernova (GEV). Because the regulated names are effectively bond proxies, this layer trades against the 10-year yield as much as against the AI story, which is why it has been the weakest part of Sheet 1 while yields climbed.

Follow a dollar of capex: it lands most heavily on the chip layer, which captures the most dollars but carries the most risk (a rival can win a socket, custom silicon can erode the moat, and an overcapacity or return-on-investment scare hits it first). The power, conduit, cooling and fiber layers are lower-binary: whatever chip and model win, the building still needs steel, copper, transformers and megawatts. That is the trade-off, highest upside in silicon, more durable margins of safety in the infrastructure beneath it. Today was a clean illustration: chips, memory and photonics all fell while electrical and steel rose.

macro_strategy.regime_label: A narrowing tape: records in the Dow, distribution in tech, and a September hike that is fading but not gone
macro_strategy.regime_detail: The quant model still reads the market as an uptrend at normal volatility, and the index level supports that, but the composition of this market changed today. The Dow closed at a record for a fifth straight session while the Nasdaq fell 0.8%, and on the board fifteen names closed at or near the top of their 30-day ranges while the only names at the very bottom were power utilities and Novo Nordisk. Three forces define it. First, energy relief keeps compounding: President Trump said a Strait of Hormuz agreement could land within days, WTI settled near $75 and Brent near $79 against roughly $84 WTI at the Jul 29 peak, the 10-year eased toward 4.6%, and September hike odds fell to about 57% from 67%. Second, leadership rotated rather than broke: healthcare rose 1.50% on heavy confirming volume and electrical and steel rose 0.25%, while memory fell 3.57%, quantum 3.48%, chip equipment 2.21% and photonics 2.18%. Third, the selling was strikingly thin. SMH fell on 0.47 times average volume, QQQ on 0.77x, SPY on 0.90x, and there were zero heavy liquidation events across all 21 ETFs. Underlying inflation continues to improve (June CPI 3.5% from 4.2%, core 2.6% from 2.8%, unemployment 4.2%, VIX 16.5), so this remains a positioning-and-expectations market layered on genuine disinflation, not a growth scare.

drivers.reading: Hawkish hold, with the hike odds easing. Fed funds 3.50-3.75%, held on a 9-to-3 vote with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissenting for a hike, and September now priced near 57% from about 67% yesterday. The 10-year eased toward 4.6% from the 4.70% print the chip still shows for Aug 3, the 2-year is 4.25%, and the 10Y-2Y curve is positively sloped by about 0.45. CFTC data through Jul 28 shows leveraged funds added 90,934 contracts to an already enormous 10-year short, so the fast money is still pressing the higher-yields bet even as the market prices it out.
drivers.playbook: Do not assume the next move is a cut, because three Fed presidents just voted against that assumption, but note the direction of travel improved today. A flat-to-higher path keeps pressure on anything valued on distant profits, which is why quantum, space, the neoclouds and pre-revenue nuclear stay sized as venture bets. The clearest expression of the rate trade on this board is the regulated utilities in section 08, which are bond proxies sitting at 30-day lows: they are the group that benefits most if the hike comes off the table, and the group that keeps bleeding if it does not. A 10-year near 4.6% also means cash still pays you to be patient, so there is no penalty for adding in tranches.

drivers.reading: Improving on both fronts. June CPI 3.5% year over year (down from 4.2%) and core 2.6% (down from 2.8%). WTI settled near $75 and Brent near $79 after President Trump said a Hormuz reopening could come within days, well below the roughly $84 peak on Jul 29. The macro strip still shows $84.25 because FRED publishes with a lag. Aug 12 is the print that decides September, and two consecutive sessions of falling crude are the single most helpful input it could have.
drivers.playbook: Do not press risk into the Aug 12 print in either direction. Cheaper crude feeds directly into a softer headline number, but it rests on a deal that has not been signed, and a collapse in the talks reverses both oil and the hike odds overnight. Own some pricing power and real assets as the hedge: market-priced power operators (CEG, VST, TLN), healthcare that passes costs through (LLY, XLV), and broad exposure via VOO or VTI. Keep some cash available for the print itself rather than deploying everything before it.

drivers.reading: Still strong where it counts for this board, and today added direct evidence. AMD's data-center revenue rose 107% year over year to $6.7 billion, now 58% of company sales, with third-quarter guidance near $13 billion. Hyperscaler capital spending is guided to roughly $725 billion for 2026, up 77%, with about $450 billion of that AI-specific, and Meta raised its range again. Memory contract prices are set to rise 50% to 55% this quarter and HBM is sold out for 2026. Unemployment 4.2% and steady.
drivers.playbook: This is the leg of the thesis that is working, so let it work rather than trading around it, and note the specific lesson from today: demand growing 107% was not enough to lift a stock that had already risen 140% this year. The response to that is not to abandon the theme but to own it through baskets where valuation risk is spread (SMH lost 1.04% on the day AMD lost 7.04%), and to size the AI hardware sleeve so a 30% to 45% drawdown is survivable, because that is what its history says it does.

drivers.reading: The dominant driver, and now the main reason for caution. Hedge funds cut US tech at a record pace into mid-July and have since posted their biggest increase in net technology exposure in more than five years, with positioning back near the highest levels since 2016. Gross leverage across the prime book is at a record and net leverage near three-year highs, with US long-short net leverage at 55.3%, in the top 11% of the past year. Mega-cap tech is roughly 19% of total US net exposure. Meanwhile today's tape needed almost no selling pressure to fall, with volume ratios of 0.47 on SMH and 0.77 on QQQ.
drivers.playbook: Use flow as a timing input only. A rebuilt, highly leveraged book means the cushion that made the last bounce easy has been spent, and leveraged holders sell because they must rather than because they choose to, which is what turns an ordinary pullback into a sharp one. Practically: slow purchases in whatever the crowd is most concentrated in, which is the mega-cap AI complex, and keep position sizes where a fast 10% move does not force you to act. The Aug 7 COT release is the next checkpoint, specifically whether the record leveraged short in the 10-year got any smaller as yields eased.

drivers.reading: Still a first-order driver, and today showed its two-way nature. The draft FCC-led ban on Chinese optical transceiver modules moved into rule drafting, with reporting emphasising that the supply-chain dependency runs both ways and that domestic contract manufacturers cannot replace Chinese capacity quickly. The optics names gave back part of yesterday's 6% to 21% surge, falling 2.18% as a group. Medicare drug price negotiation is in its third cycle, reaching Part B drugs for the first time, with comments closing Aug 17 and prices effective 2028. Government equity stakes and anchor-customer relationships continue to underwrite Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas, Centrus, BWX Technologies, Rocket Lab and Palantir.
drivers.playbook: Let policy adjust your sizing, never form your thesis. The optics chain rising 21% on a draft rule and giving part of it back within 48 hours, with nothing in the rule having changed, is the cleanest evidence available that these are probability repricings rather than value changes. Prefer businesses that would work without the rule and get helped by it (Coherent, Fabrinet, Corning) over ones that only work because of it. Keep the GOV-badged names a slice rather than a concentration, since the same administration that created the floor can remove it.

macro_strategy.positioning: The stance is unchanged, and the consistency is deliberate: a session in which the Dow set a record and the Nasdaq fell 0.8% is noise against a ten-year plan. Keep the diversified core (VOO or VTI) as the largest position and keep adding on schedule. Today made the case for it about as clearly as a quiet day can: the index absorbed a 12% collapse in Astera Labs and a 7% drop in AMD after a record quarter and finished essentially flat, because healthcare and industrials paid for it. Treat the thin volume behind the decline as a reason not to expect a bargain rather than a reason to rush, since nothing was genuinely liquidated. The most interesting value on the board remains established nuclear infrastructure, where four names closed at the very bottom of their 30-day ranges while twenty-year hyperscaler contracts sit underneath them, and where the weakness is best explained by the 10-year yield rather than by anything operational. That group is a candidate to accumulate patiently, not to buy in one lump, because the downtrend is still active. Keep the healthcare sleeve (LLY, XLV), which today was leadership rather than shelter and is the part of the portfolio least connected to hyperscaler spending, the oil price and the September decision. Keep Sheet 2 sized as venture bets: quantum fell 3.48% today and the space names are being pushed around by a SpaceX lockup expiry rather than by their own progress. Hold some cash for the Aug 12 CPI print rather than deploying it all before.

scenarios.trigger: If the Hormuz deal is signed and the Aug 12 CPI print lands soft
scenarios.response: The September hike gets priced out entirely, the 10-year eases from the mid-4s, and the rotation reverses in favour of exactly what has been sold. The groups with the most room are the ones furthest below their 50-day averages: the regulated utilities and merchant power names in section 08, memory, chip equipment (KLA is 12.97% below its 50-day, Lam 9.13%) and the space names. The mistake to avoid is waiting for the confirmation and buying only after the move.

scenarios.trigger: If the Hormuz talks collapse and oil goes back toward $90
scenarios.response: Hike odds jump back above the 67% they carried yesterday, the 10-year pushes toward 4.75% or higher, and this time the market meets that shock with a rebuilt, highly leveraged book rather than the empty one it had two weeks ago. Expect the sharpest damage in the mega-cap AI complex where positioning is most crowded, and in the rate-sensitive utilities that are already at their lows. Healthcare, dividend value (SCHD) and the diversified core are what hold up. This is the scenario that rewards having added on a schedule rather than in one lump.

scenarios.trigger: If the Fed hikes in September
scenarios.response: The long-duration parts of the board reprice first: quantum, space, the neoclouds and any name whose profits are mostly in the future. Anything valued on cash flow today holds better, which means healthcare and the dividend sleeve. The regulated utilities are the awkward case, because they are cheap on trend but are the most direct casualty of higher yields, so they would likely get cheaper before they recover. A hike would also vindicate the record leveraged short in the 10-year, so expect the bond move to be fast. Nothing on this page should be sold in anticipation: a single 25 basis-point move does not change a decade-long thesis, it changes the price you pay this quarter.

scenarios.trigger: If a hyperscaler cuts its capital-spending guidance
scenarios.response: This is the one that actually matters, and it still has not happened. Roughly $725 billion of committed 2026 spending is the floor under every supplier on Sheet 1, and Meta raised its range again in the latest round. The theme does not break when a supplier misses, and it did not break today when AMD fell 7% on a record quarter. It breaks when a buyer cuts the budget. Watch hyperscaler margin commentary for the first sign, and note that Alphabet's 4.03% fall today was partly about capex pressure on margins, which is the pressure that would eventually produce such a cut. If it comes, reduce single-name AI hardware exposure first and let the diversified core and healthcare carry the portfolio.

watchlist_notes: Two sheets, same columns. Sheet 1 is the established, large-dollar side across ten sections: semis and fab, chip equipment, memory and storage, servers and cooling, fiber optics and cabling, photonics and optical interconnect, electrical and steel, nuclear infrastructure and power majors, big tech, and healthcare. Sheet 2 is the smaller-dollar speculative side (nuclear developers and fuel, quantum, space and defense, government-backed materials and small AI infra, neoclouds). Read the Bull Score first: it is six checks on whether the long-term case holds, and hovering it shows which checks passed. What the board looks like at the Aug 5 close: 45 of 70 names finished lower, and only three of fifteen groups finished higher. Healthcare led at +1.50%, followed by government-backed materials at +0.39% and electrical and steel at +0.25%. The laggards were memory and storage at -3.57%, quantum at -3.48%, the neoclouds at -2.59%, chip equipment at -2.21% and photonics at -2.18%, the last giving back part of yesterday's policy-driven surge. Thirteen names closed at 95% or more of their 30-day range, and the list is revealing: Nvidia, Broadcom, Arista, Coherent, Microsoft, Oracle, Dell, Centrus and five of the six electrical and steel names (Eaton, Atkore, WESCO, Hubbell, Nucor). Only six names sit at 10% or less of their range, and five of those are power companies (Vistra, Dominion, PSEG and Entergy all at 0%, Southern at 4%), with Novo Nordisk the sixth at 3%. The volume flag is unusually clear today and it is a constructive one: this decline had almost no participation, with SMH trading 0.47 times its average, QQQ 0.77x and SPY 0.90x, and zero heavy liquidation events across all 21 ETFs against several yesterday. Only seven individual names carry a heavy liquidation event at all. What has not healed is accumulated distribution: SanDisk 11 days, TSMC 9, Cameco 9, Vistra 8, Oracle 8, Intel 8, and at fund level SMH 9, SOXX 8 and VGT 8 against just one for VOO. Sheet 2 was weak across the board, and the space names are being moved by the SpaceX post-IPO lockup expiring Aug 6, which raises the tradable share count by more than 140%, rather than by anything operational: size them like venture bets, not positions.
